patient.chief_complaint: Confusion and agitation in known alcoholic cirrhosis — rifaximin non-adherence, fever
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. T. is a 64-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 18), prior HE episode, and a robust HE prophylaxis regimen, brought by his sister for acute confusion and agitation over the past 3 days. She confirmed he had been out of rifaximin for 10 days due to an insurance authorization issue. Over the prior 5 days he had 4-5 loose stools/day — attributed initially to lactulose; however combined with a low-grade fever and recent respiratory illness 2 weeks prior, the possibility of infectious GI precipitant was considered. His ammonia is 142 µmol/L — markedly elevated. EEG shows classic triphasic waves. CT head is normal. The precipitants are clear: (1) rifaximin non-adherence x 10 days (primary — gut bacteria overgrowth without rifaximin suppression), (2) low-grade fever suggesting possible infection, (3) diarrhea-associated electrolyte loss. This is a straightforward HE case.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy, grade 3, alcoholic cirrhosis — precipitated by rifaximin non-adherence x 10 days (insurance gap) + hypokalemia from diarrhea; ammonia 142 µmol/L; classic EEG triphasic waves

differential.key_features: PMN 124 — SBP excluded; leukocytosis 13.6 from HE stress response and diarrhea infection; culture negative
Ethanol negative (< 10 mg/dL); sister confirms sobriety; rifaximin non-adherence is the identified precipitant
Creatinine 1.3 (mild AKI from dehydration) — not severe enough for uremic encephalopathy; ammonia 142 and liver disease are diagnostic for HE

optimal_actions.action: Labs — ammonia, LFTs, CBC, electrolytes, toxicology; identify rifaximin non-adherence from history
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia 142, hypokalemia 3.2, WBC 13.6 — rifaximin gap + hypokalemia as precipitants

optimal_actions.action: EEG — classic triphasic waves confirm HE; exclude NCSE
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Classic frontal triphasic waves — grade 3 HE confirmed

optimal_actions.action: Restart rifaximin + lactulose optimization + KCl IV repletion

critical_actions: Medication history must include adherence — rifaximin non-adherence for 10 days (insurance issue) is the primary precipitant; identifying and addressing barriers to medication access is a critical care intervention
Classic EEG triphasic waves in HE do NOT represent epilepsy — they are metabolic and should not be treated with antiepileptics
SBP must be excluded despite PMN below threshold — culture was negative; reassuring
Second overt HE episode warrants transplant evaluation — MELD 21 with 2 episodes
contraindicated_actions: Treating EEG triphasic waves with antiepileptics — they are metabolic, not epileptic
Holding lactulose due to diarrhea without adjusting dose — diarrhea must be distinguished from lactulose-titrated stools
key_reasoning_points: Rifaximin non-adherence (even 10 days) allows gut bacterial overgrowth → ammonia surge → HE in cirrhotic patients; insurance barriers are a real clinical problem causing preventable HE
Hypokalemia + rifaximin non-adherence together produce additive ammonia elevation — hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis independently
Two overt HE episodes is a clinical threshold for transplant evaluation — identifies patients with significantly reduced 1-year survival without transplant
Classic EEG triphasic waves are diagnostic for HE — they are metabolic, not epileptiform; do not treat with antiepileptics unless NCSE is identified

red_herrings.intended_effect: Diagnose as SBP or other infection as primary cause; initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics; delay HE-specific treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: SBP excluded by paracentesis PMN 124; leukocytosis and fever are from HE stress response + diarrheal illness; rifaximin non-adherence is the primary HE precipitant; antibiotics not indicated

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute diarrhea to lactulose overdose and REDUCE lactulose; increase stool-hardening agents; worsen HE by under-treating it
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: This patient is OFF rifaximin for 10 days — the primary problem is under-treatment of gut flora, not lactulose overdose; lactulose should be maintained at 30 mL BID-TID targeting 2-3 soft stools, and rifaximin restarted immediately; the diarrhea is from the GI illness, not from lactulose overdose
